title: 1 Kings 8:22–53
context: Standing before the altar with hands spread toward heaven, Solomon prays at length. He praises the LORD as the covenant-keeping God without equal and asks Him to keep His promise of a continuing throne for David’s line, if David’s sons walk faithfully. He confesses that heaven itself cannot contain God, yet asks that His eyes be open toward this house and that He hear from heaven and forgive. Seven petitions follow, covering oaths and justice, defeat, drought, famine and plague, the foreigner, war, and exile. Many readers note that these situations echo the covenant warnings of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. The prayer closes by appealing to Israel’s status as the LORD’s inheritance, brought out of Egypt. The parallel account is 2 Chronicles 6:12–42.

verses.text: Solomon stood before the LORD’s altar in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven;
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon stands before the altar with hands spread toward heaven. Arminian readers note the posture of open, dependent prayer, as the king places himself before God in the sight of all Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king acting as the people’s representative before God, a role fitting the covenant setting. Both traditions read the posture as humble prayer directed to heaven, not to the building itself.

verses.text: and he said, “LORD, the God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above, or on earth beneath; who keeps covenant and loving kindness with your servants who walk before you with all their heart;
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon confesses that no God is like the LORD, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who walk before Him with all their heart. Arminian readers note the link between God’s faithfulness and wholehearted walking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s loving kindness as the source of His people’s faithful walk. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as praise for God’s unique covenant faithfulness, with whole-hearted devotion as the fitting response.

verses.text: who has kept with your servant David my father that which you promised him. Yes, you spoke with your mouth, and have fulfilled it with your hand, as it is today.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon says God has kept His promise to David, speaking with His mouth and fulfilling with His hand. Arminian readers see the present day as evidence that God’s word is trustworthy and that He acts on it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same: God’s spoken promise and His acts are one, as the temple standing before them shows. Both traditions read the verse as grounding the requests that follow in what God has already done.

verses.text: Now therefore, may LORD, the God of Israel, keep with your servant David my father that which you have promised him, saying, ‘There shall not fail from you a man in my sight to sit on the throne of Israel, if only your children take heed to their way, to walk before me as you have walked before me.’
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to keep His promise of a continuing throne, if David’s sons walk faithfully. Arminian readers note the conditional wording and see real responsibility placed on each king. Each king must take heed to his way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hold the conditional together with the unconditional promise of 2 Samuel 7, as this site has treated the Davidic covenant as shared ground. Shared ground: both traditions read the condition as a real call to faithfulness.

verses.text: “Now therefore, God of Israel, please let your word be verified, which you spoke to your servant David my father.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to let His word to David be verified. Arminian readers see a prayer that takes God’s promise seriously and asks Him to continue fulfilling it in the generations still to come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see prayer for what God has promised as a fitting way to receive His faithfulness. Both traditions read the verse as an appeal to God’s own word, in which the king asks for what God has already said He will do.

verses.text: But will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks whether God will truly dwell on earth, since heaven cannot contain Him. Arminian readers see humility before God’s greatness, keeping the temple from being thought of as a container for God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a clear statement of God’s transcendence, joined to His gracious choice to make His name dwell among His people. Shared ground: both traditions read this verse as a key safeguard, compare Isaiah 66:1 by reference.

verses.text: Yet have respect for the prayer of your servant and for his supplication, LORD my God, to listen to the cry and to the prayer which your servant prays before you today;
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to respect his prayer and hear his cry today. Arminian readers see sincere petition that seeks God’s attention, consistent with God genuinely hearing and responding to His people’s requests.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see prayer as the means God has appointed for His people to seek Him. Both traditions agree that God truly hears; on how prayer relates to God’s plan, see the existing contrast at Joshua 10:14 rather than a new one here.

verses.text: that your eyes may be open toward this house night and day, even toward the place of which you have said, ‘My name shall be there;’ to listen to the prayer which your servant prays toward this place.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks that God’s eyes be open toward this house night and day, the place where He said His name would be. Arminian readers see a request for God’s continual attention to His people’s prayers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the name dwelling in the house as God’s chosen way of being present, recalling Deuteronomy 12:5, 11. Shared ground: both traditions read the request as the foundation for the petitions that follow, all directed toward this place.

verses.text: Listen to the supplication of your servant, and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. Yes, hear in heaven, your dwelling place; and when you hear, forgive.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to hear in heaven, His dwelling place, and when He hears, to forgive. Arminian readers note that forgiveness is the first and central request, showing that Israel’s deepest need is mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated phrase “hear in heaven” as keeping God’s true dwelling above, with the temple as the place toward which prayer is made. Both traditions read forgiveness as the heart of the whole prayer, agreed by both.

verses.text: “If a man sins against his neighbor, and an oath is laid on him to cause him to swear, and he comes and swears before your altar in this house,
verses.arminianNotes: The first petition concerns a man who sins against his neighbor and swears an oath at the altar. Arminian readers note that the temple serves justice in everyday disputes, not only national crises.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the final judge over oaths made in His name. Shared ground: both traditions read the petition as asking God to uphold truth in cases that human courts cannot settle, compare Exodus 22:10–11 by reference.

verses.text: then hear in heaven, and act, and judge your servants, condemning the wicked, to bring his way on his own head, and justifying the righteous, to give him according to his righteousness.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to judge, condemning the wicked and justifying the righteous. Arminian readers see God’s justice applied to each person according to their actions, bringing each one’s way on their own head.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s justice as perfect, discerning what human judges cannot see. Both traditions read the verse as a plea for righteous judgment, with God trusted to distinguish truly between the guilty and the innocent.

verses.text: “When your people Israel are struck down before the enemy because they have sinned against you, if they turn again to you and confess your name, and pray and make supplication to you in this house,
verses.arminianNotes: When Israel is defeated because of sin, if they turn, confess, and pray, Solomon asks God to hear. Arminian readers see repentance as a real response that God invites and to which He graciously answers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see turning and confession as fruits of God’s grace at work in His people. Both traditions agree that this petition calls for real repentance; on how repentance relates to God’s response, see the existing contrast at Judges 10:16.

verses.text: then hear in heaven, and forgive the sin of your people Israel, and bring them again to the land which you gave to their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to forgive and bring them back to the land. Arminian readers note the restoration of the land as part of God’s covenant mercy, returning His people to what He had given their fathers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see restoration as God’s faithfulness to His promise even after His people have sinned. Shared ground: both traditions read the petition as rooted in God’s covenant with the fathers, joining forgiveness to restoration.

verses.text: “When the sky is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and confess your name, and turn from their sin when you afflict them,
verses.arminianNotes: When there is no rain because of sin, if they pray, confess, and turn, Solomon asks God to hear. Arminian readers note the echo of covenant warnings about drought (compare Deuteronomy 11:16–17) and the call to turn from sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see affliction as a means God uses to bring His people back. Both traditions read the drought petition as connecting creation’s gifts to Israel’s covenant faithfulness, with repentance as the way back to blessing.

verses.text: then hear in heaven, and forgive the sin of your servants, and of your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk; and send rain on your land which you have given to your people for an inheritance.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to forgive, teach them the good way, and send rain. Arminian readers note that forgiveness is joined to instruction, showing that God’s mercy aims at a renewed way of life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s teaching as part of His gracious work in restoring His people. Shared ground: both traditions read the petition as seeking more than relief, asking that God guide His people in the way they should walk.

verses.text: “If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence, if there is blight, mildew, locust or caterpillar; if their enemy besieges them in the land of their cities, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is,
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon lists famine, pestilence, blight, mildew, locust, siege, plague, and sickness. Arminian readers note the wide range of disasters covered, showing that no trouble falls outside the scope of prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the list the many forms of covenant discipline described in Deuteronomy 28. Both traditions read the verse as affirming that every kind of calamity can be brought before God in prayer toward His house.

verses.text: whatever prayer and supplication is made by any man, or by all your people Israel, who shall each know the plague of his own heart, and spread out his hands toward this house,
verses.arminianNotes: Prayer may come from any individual or the whole people, each knowing the plague of his own heart. Arminian readers see personal responsibility and self-examination as part of genuine prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see “the plague of his own heart” as recognizing that the deepest trouble lies within, not only in outward disaster. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as calling for honest awareness of sin before God.

verses.text: then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive, and act, and give to every man according to all his ways, whose heart you know (for you, even you only, know the hearts of all the children of men);
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to forgive and give to each according to his ways, since God alone knows every heart. Arminian readers see God’s knowledge as the basis for just and merciful treatment of each person.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession that God alone knows the heart as humbling all human judgment. Both traditions read the verse as affirming God’s perfect knowledge of people’s inner lives, a point fully shared by both.

verses.text: that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land which you gave to our fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: The goal is that they may fear God all their days in the land. Arminian readers see the purpose of forgiveness as a renewed reverence that shapes the whole of life in response to God’s mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fear of the LORD as the fruit of forgiveness, compare Psalm 130:4 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that mercy leads to reverence rather than to careless living.

verses.text: “Moreover, concerning the foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, when he comes out of a far country for your name’s sake
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon prays for the foreigner who comes from a far country for the LORD’s name. Arminian readers see God’s welcome extended beyond Israel to anyone who seeks Him, a theme developed in Isaiah 56:6–7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see this petition as anticipating the nations being drawn to God, in line with the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3). Both traditions read the verse as a remarkable openness toward outsiders who come in faith.

verses.text: (for they shall hear of your great name and of your mighty hand and of your outstretched arm), when he comes and prays toward this house,
verses.arminianNotes: The foreigner will hear of God’s great name, mighty hand, and outstretched arm. Arminian readers see God’s acts in Israel’s history becoming a witness that draws people from far away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s fame among the nations as part of His purpose to make His name known. Shared ground: both traditions read the parenthesis as explaining why foreigners would come, recalling the exodus language of Deuteronomy 4:34.

verses.text: hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and do according to all that the foreigner calls to you for; that all the peoples of the earth may know your name, to fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house which I have built is called by your name.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to answer the foreigner so that all peoples may know His name and fear Him as Israel does. Arminian readers see a universal purpose in God’s dealings with Israel, extending His mercy to all nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same purpose and stress that it is God’s name that draws the nations. Both traditions agree that the temple serves God’s purpose of making Himself known among all peoples, a point both treat as shared ground.

verses.text: “If your people go out to battle against their enemy, by whatever way you shall send them, and they pray to the LORD toward the city which you have chosen, and toward the house which I have built for your name,
verses.arminianNotes: When Israel goes to battle where God sends them and prays toward the city and house, Solomon asks for help. Arminian readers note that the petition assumes Israel goes where God sends, not in wars of its own choosing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see dependence on God in battle as a mark of faithful kingship. Shared ground: both traditions read the petition as asking for God’s help in conflicts He has directed, with prayer turned toward His chosen place.

verses.text: then hear in heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to hear and maintain their cause. Arminian readers see God as the defender of His people when they act in obedience and seek His aid in prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God upholding the cause of His people as part of His covenant faithfulness. Both traditions read the short verse as a plea for God’s justice and protection in war, without assuming victory is automatic.

verses.text: If they sin against you (for there is no man who doesn’t sin), and you are angry with them and deliver them to the enemy, so that they carry them away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near;
verses.arminianNotes: If they sin, for there is no man who does not sin, and are taken captive, Solomon prays. Arminian readers affirm the universality of sin that the parenthesis states; see the existing contrasts at Psalm 53:3 and Genesis 6:5.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the parenthesis as a plain statement that all people sin (compare Ecclesiastes 7:20 by reference). Shared ground: both traditions agree on sin’s universality here; their difference on human inability is already set out in those boxes.

verses.text: yet if they repent in the land where they are carried captive, and turn again, and make supplication to you in the land of those who carried them captive, saying, ‘We have sinned and have done perversely; we have dealt wickedly,’
verses.arminianNotes: If they repent in the land of captivity and confess that they have sinned, done perversely, and dealt wickedly, Solomon asks God to hear. Arminian readers see a real turning of heart, even far from the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the threefold confession as an honest acknowledgment of guilt, the kind of repentance God’s grace produces. Both traditions read the petition as anticipating exile and showing that repentance is possible wherever God’s people are.

verses.text: if they return to you with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies who carried them captive, and pray to you toward their land which you gave to their fathers, the city which you have chosen and the house which I have built for your name,
verses.arminianNotes: If they return with all their heart and soul and pray toward the land, city, and house, Solomon asks God to hear. Arminian readers note the echo of Deuteronomy 4:29–31, where wholehearted seeking leads to God’s mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wholehearted return as the work of God’s grace in His people, in keeping with Deuteronomy 30:6. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing genuine repentance, directed toward God’s chosen place even from exile.

verses.text: then hear their prayer and their supplication in heaven, your dwelling place, and maintain their cause;
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to hear their prayer in heaven and maintain their cause. Arminian readers note that the same request made for battle in 8:45 is now made for exiles, showing God’s care in every circumstance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s dwelling in heaven as the guarantee that His people’s prayers are heard even when the temple is far away. Both traditions read the verse as an appeal to God’s justice on behalf of His repentant people.

verses.text: and forgive your people who have sinned against you, and all their transgressions in which they have transgressed against you; and give them compassion before those who carried them captive, that they may have compassion on them
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to forgive and to give His people compassion before their captors. Arminian readers see God’s mercy reaching even into the hearts of foreign rulers on behalf of His people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s power to move the hearts of captors as part of His providence, compare Ezra 1:1 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the request as seeking forgiveness and practical mercy in exile.

verses.text: (for they are your people and your inheritance, which you brought out of Egypt, from the middle of the iron furnace);
verses.arminianNotes: They are God’s people and inheritance, brought out of Egypt, the iron furnace. Arminian readers see the appeal grounded in God’s past act of redemption and His relationship with His people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal resting on God’s own choice and redemption, not on Israel’s merit. Both traditions read the image of the iron furnace, also found in Deuteronomy 4:20, as recalling the harshness of slavery and the greatness of deliverance.

verses.text: that your eyes may be open to the supplication of your servant and to the supplication of your people Israel, to listen to them whenever they cry to you.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks that God’s eyes be open to the prayers of king and people whenever they cry. Arminian readers note that the prayer returns to its opening theme in 8:29, asking for God’s continual attention.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s attentiveness as an expression of His covenant faithfulness to the people He has made His own. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as drawing the prayer toward its close with a request for God to hear.

verses.text: For you separated them from among all the peoples of the earth to be your inheritance, as you spoke by Moses your servant, when you brought our fathers out of Egypt, Lord GOD.”
verses.arminianNotes: God separated Israel from all peoples to be His inheritance, as He spoke through Moses. Arminian readers see Israel’s calling as a gracious choice for a purpose, including witness to the nations (8:43).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s choice of Israel as rooted in His own will, compare Exodus 19:5–6 by reference. Both traditions read the verse as the prayer’s final ground; on wider questions of election, they point to existing contrasts rather than adding one here.
